summary: Defines the application/whoispp-query media type. Together with RFC 2958, it lets MIME-aware mail software and other systems carry Whois++ transactions.

plainLanguage.summary: Whois++ is a lookup service for people and things. This gives its questions a label so email can carry them.

questions: how to send whois++ queries in mime
subtitle: Registers a MIME type that carries Whois++ queries, so email and other MIME systems can ask Whois++ questions.

tldr.problem: Whois++ queries had no standard way to travel inside MIME-aware mail software and other systems that use Internet media types.
tldr.mechanism: The memo registers the media type application/whoispp-query and gives an ABNF grammar for the set of acceptable Whois++ server input, which is what a query object contains.
tldr.outcome: Together with RFC 2958, which covers the answers, MIME software can carry complete Whois++ transactions. The type has no native authentication.

today: RFC 2957 is an Informational memo and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion for answers is RFC 2958.

sections.title: What the Type Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2957 defines how queries of the Whois++ protocol (RFC 1835) are expressed as a MIME media type (RFC 2046). Its stated aim, together with RFC 2958, is to let MIME-enabled mail software, and other systems that use Internet media types, carry out Whois++ transactions.

This memo covers the question half of the exchange. The answers are covered by the companion type, application/whoispp-response.
sections.plainLanguage: One memo labels the questions and its sister memo labels the answers, so mail programs can carry both.

sections.title: The MIME Registration
sections.content: Section 1 of the RFC is a registration template addressed to IANA. The type name is application and the subtype is whoispp-query. There are no required parameters and no optional parameters, and any valid MIME encodings may be used. The published specification is the RFC itself, the contact is the first author, and the intended usage is common.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the form that gets the new label added to the official list of labels.

sections.title: Query Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar, written in the ABNF of RFC 2234, defines the acceptable input to a Whois++ server, and so the structure of a whoispp-query object. Rule names and string literals are US-ASCII and case-insensitive.

A command is either a system-command (such as constraints, describe, commands, version, list, show, help or ?) or search terms optionally followed by a colon and global constraints, ending in a CR LF. Terms combine with or, and and not, and parentheses can group them. A term can be a general string, or a specific one such as handle=, value= or template=, or an attribute name with a value.

Blanks that matter to a query must be escaped. A few characters, namely : ; , ( ) = !, may be preceded or followed by a single blank when significant.
sections.plainLanguage: The grammar is the rulebook for how to word a question so the server understands it, such as "find this AND that".

sections.title: Constraints on a Search
sections.content:
Constraints shape how a search runs. Global constraints, after the colon and separated by semicolons, include format (full, abridged, handle, summary or server-to-ask), maxfull, maxhits, case and search. Optional global constraints add authenticate, language, incharset, outcharset, ignore and include.

Local constraints attach to a single term and are limited to case (ignore or consider) and search (exact, substring, regex, fuzzy or lstring). Character sets include us-ascii, the iso-8859 family and UTF-8; the older UTF-8 labels are kept for compatibility with older Whois++ servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Constraints are extra instructions on the question, like "only give me five answers" or "match the spelling exactly".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The type carries purely descriptive information with no directives. The RFC notes security concerns about the appropriateness (privacy) of the information provided and about the authenticity of that information. The content type provides no native mechanisms for authentication, although the grammar has an optional authenticate constraint that names a method.
sections.plainLanguage: The label does not prove who sent a question, so anyone handling private information has to be careful.

data.title: Query grammar (excerpt)
data.code:
whois-command   =   ( system-command / terms [":" globalcnstrnts] )
                    nl

terms           =   and-expr *("or" and-expr)

and-expr        =   not-expr *("and" not-expr)

not-expr        =   ["not"] (term / ( "(" terms ")" ))

specificname    =   "handle" / "value" / "template"
